project.title: NYC Airbnb Market Intelligence
project.subtitle: Exploring Listing Prices, Room Types, Neighbourhood Patterns and Availability in New York City
project.dataset_name: New York City Airbnb Open Data (2019)

cleaning_summary.action: Filled 16 missing names and 21 host names with 'Unknown'
Created log_price = np.log1p(price_capped) for Gaussian modeling

questions.title: Overall Distribution of Listing Prices & Log-Transformation
questions.concept: Measures of Central Tendency, Skewness, Kurtosis, and Normalization
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding the empirical price distribution determines whether standard parametric models (like Ordinary Least Squares regression) can be directly applied without violating the classical Gauss-Markov assumption of homoscedasticity and normality of residuals.

variables_and_units.price_capped: Winsorized price capped at 99th percentile ($799 USD)

questions.analytical_method: Comparison of parametric moments (arithmetic mean, standard deviation, Fisher-Pearson skewness, and excess kurtosis) against robust non-parametric estimators (median, IQR) and logarithmic normalization.
questions.graph_interpretation: The raw price histogram shows severe positive skewness (19.12) with a massive disparity between the mean ($152.76) and median ($106.00), driven by luxury listings stretching to $10,000. Applying 99th percentile capping ($799) reduces skewness to 2.78, while natural log-transformation ln(1 + price) produces near-symmetric bell curve behavior (0.37 skewness) centered at 4.73.
questions.conclusion: Listing prices follow an empirical log-normal distribution. The median ($106) provides an uncorrupted measure of central market tendency, and log(price) must be utilized as the target variable for linear econometric modeling.

statistical_test.result: Reject pure normality; log(price) significantly stabilizes variance relative to raw price.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: 99th-percentile capping intentionally right-censors the top 1% of ultra-luxury penthouses to eliminate high-leverage outliers, underestimating peak luxury revenue.

questions.title: Listing Price Disparities Across NYC Boroughs
questions.concept: Five-Number Summary, Comparative Boxplots, and Interquartile Range (IQR)
questions.why_it_matters: Spatial price stratification across administrative submarkets reveals regional premium boundaries, enabling hosts to benchmark local rates and travelers to identify budget zones.
questions.analytical_method: Five-number summary calculation (Minimum, Q25, Median, Q75, Maximum) and Interquartile Range (IQR = Q75 - Q25) dispersion analysis across all 5 borough groups.
questions.graph_interpretation: Manhattan exhibits both the highest median price ($150) and the widest dispersion (IQR = $125, Q25 = $95, Q75 = $220). Brooklyn forms a distinct second tier ($90 median, $119.43 mean). Queens ($75) and Staten Island ($75) follow, while Bronx offers the most affordable accommodation ($65 median).
questions.conclusion: Geographic borough is the primary geographic driver of accommodation rates. Manhattan listings command a 66.7% premium over Brooklyn and a 130.8% premium over Bronx.

statistical_test.result: p < 1e-300: Overwhelming evidence that price distributions differ systematically across boroughs.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Aggregating by borough masks substantial micro-neighbourhood variance within boroughs (e.g. DUMBO vs East New York in Brooklyn).

questions.title: Impact of Room Type on Accommodation Pricing
questions.concept: Categorical Stratification and Mean/Median Margin Comparison
questions.why_it_matters: Quantifies the monetary value that the short-term rental market places on physical privacy and spatial exclusivity.

variables_and_units.room_type: Exclusivity category (Entire home/apt, Private room, Shared room)

questions.analytical_method: Categorical stratification comparing mean and median prices, standard deviations, and pairwise price ratios.
questions.graph_interpretation: Entire homes/apartments average $198.35/night (median $160), Private rooms average $86.03/night (median $70), and Shared rooms average $68.61/night (median $45). Entire homes command a 2.31x premium over private rooms and 2.89x over shared rooms.
questions.conclusion: Room exclusivity is the single strongest property-level determinant of price, far outweighing number of reviews or host listing count.

statistical_test.result: t = 175.88, p < 1e-300: Large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.61).

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Room type is self-reported by hosts and does not standardize for total square footage or bedroom count.

questions.title: Room Type Composition and Proportions Across Boroughs
questions.concept: Contingency Analysis, Proportional Cross-Tabulation, and Segmented Stacked Visualizations
questions.why_it_matters: Reveals whether urban submarkets function primarily as tourist whole-unit hotels or local resident home-sharing ecosystems.
questions.analytical_method: Bivariate contingency table cross-tabulation normalized row-wise into 100% relative percentage distributions.
questions.graph_interpretation: Manhattan has the highest concentration of Entire home/apt units (60.9%), serving business and tourist travelers. Brooklyn exhibits a balanced split (47.6% Entire home, 50.4% Private room). Outer boroughs shift dramatically toward single-room rentals: Queens is 59.5% Private room, and Bronx is 59.7% Private room.
questions.conclusion: The NYC Airbnb market is bifurcated: Manhattan functions as a commercial whole-apartment lodging submarket, whereas Queens and the Bronx primarily host spare-room resident sublets.

statistical_test.result: chi^2 = 1557.95, df = 8, p < 1e-300 (Cramer's V = 0.126): Room type is strongly dependent on borough.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Does not differentiate between primary residences rented temporarily versus commercial multi-unit residential apartment conversions.

questions.title: Top 10 Most Expensive Neighbourhoods (Sample Threshold n >= 25)
questions.concept: Sample Size Thresholding, Small-Sample Bias Control, and Robust Ranking
questions.why_it_matters: Enforcing a sample size cutoff (n >= 25) prevents ultra-small luxury anomalies (e.g. a single $1,000 villa in a quiet residential district) from distorting market rankings.

variables_and_units.count: Number of active listings in sample

questions.analytical_method: Aggregation of median and mean prices grouped by micro-neighbourhood, filtered by n >= 25, and sorted descending by median price.
questions.graph_interpretation: 100% of the top 10 most expensive statistically supported neighbourhoods in NYC (all located in Manhattan) are: Tribeca ($295 median, n=177), NoHo ($250 median, n=78), Flatiron District ($225 median, n=80), Midtown ($210 median, n=1544), West Village ($200 median, n=768), Financial District ($200 median, n=744), Chelsea ($199 median, n=1113), SoHo ($199 median, n=358), Greenwich Village ($198 median, n=390), Battery Park City ($195 median, n=69).
questions.conclusion: High-value accommodation tightly clusters in Lower and Midtown Manhattan's historic, culinary, and commercial cores.

statistical_test.result: ANOVA F = 18.17 (p = 4.17e-30): Significant price variance even within Manhattan's elite luxury tier.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: The threshold n >= 25 excludes micro-enclaves like Fort Wadsworth (n=1, $800) and Sea Gate (n=7, $487) which lack sufficient statistical power.

questions.title: Relationship Between Annual Availability and Listing Price
questions.concept: Bivariate Correlation (Pearson r, Spearman rho) and Trend Line Analysis
questions.why_it_matters: Tests whether properties available full-time command premium commercial rates compared to occasionally shared primary residences.

variables_and_units.availability_365: Days available for booking per year (0-365)

questions.analytical_method: Bivariate linear Pearson correlation (r) and monotonic rank Spearman correlation (rho), paired with cohort decile trend profiling.
questions.graph_interpretation: Annual availability exhibits a statistically significant weak-to-moderate positive correlation with price (Pearson r = 0.1232, Spearman rho = 0.0862, p < 1e-100). The decile chart reveals that listings open year-round (330-365 days) command a median price of $130 (mean $167.35), compared to $95 median (mean $132.84) for listings with low availability (0-36 days).
questions.conclusion: High annual calendar availability signifies commercially dedicated investment inventory priced at a substantial premium over casual home-shares.

statistical_test.result: p < 1e-94: Significant positive association between availability and nightly rates.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Availability counts include days unbooked by guests as well as days blocked by hosts for personal maintenance.

questions.title: Total Review Accumulation vs. Monthly Review Velocity
questions.concept: Cumulative Metric vs Velocity Metric Correlation and Plateau Dynamics
questions.why_it_matters: Distinguishes long-tenured veteran listings with historical reviews from newer listings experiencing rapid current booking turnover.
questions.analytical_method: Pearson and Spearman bivariate correlation alongside binned velocity trajectory analysis across total review brackets.
questions.graph_interpretation: Total reviews and monthly review velocity exhibit strong positive correlation (r = 0.5893, Spearman rho = 0.851, p < 1e-300). Average monthly velocity climbs rapidly from 0.29 reviews/month for listings with 0-5 revs to 3.70 reviews/month for listings with 120-300 revs, after which review velocity plateaus due to calendar occupancy limits.
questions.conclusion: Review velocity represents recent booking turnover, while cumulative reviews reflect listing maturity and market tenure.

statistical_test.result: p < 1e-300: High monotonic concordance between tenure volume and monthly booking velocity.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Listings with zero reviews were imputed with 0.0 reviews/month; review submission rates vary based on guest propensity to review.

questions.title: Minimum Nights Requirement by Room Type & Regulatory MDL Cutoff
questions.concept: Regulatory Compliance Boundaries, Stay Duration Distributions, and Strategic Policy Shifts
questions.why_it_matters: New York State's Multiple Dwelling Law (MDL) prohibits unhosted rentals under 30 days in class-A multiple dwellings. Tracking minimum nights reveals how hosts adapt booking policy for regulatory avoidance.
questions.analytical_method: Stratified stay duration analysis computing medians, means, and percentage compliance with the 30-day MDL boundary.
questions.graph_interpretation: Entire homes enforce higher minimum stay policies (median 3 nights, mean 8.28 nights) than Private rooms (median 2 nights, mean 5.27 nights). Crucially, 12.4% of Entire homes and 5.6% of Private rooms (4,491 total listings across NYC, 9.2% of the market) mandate stays of >= 30 nights, forming a distinct secondary spike at exactly 30 days.
questions.conclusion: Hosts strategically utilize >= 30-night minimum requirements to convert illegal short-term apartments into medium-term executive and student rentals exempt from municipal short-term rental bans.

statistical_test.test_name: Mann-Whitney U Test on Stay Durations
statistical_test.result: p < 1e-120: Entire home stays are systematically longer than private room bookings.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Extreme minimum nights over 365 were pre-filtered during cleaning as booking errors.

questions.title: Host Ownership Portfolio Concentration: Individual vs Commercial
questions.concept: Market Concentration, Categorical Binning, and Portfolio Distribution
questions.why_it_matters: Evaluates the degree to which short-term housing inventory is controlled by residential single-unit homeowners versus commercial corporate property managers.

variables_and_units.calculated_host_listings_count: Total listings operated by the host across NYC (count)
variables_and_units.host_type: Binned host segment (Single Property, Multi-Listing, Commercial Host)

questions.analytical_method: Categorical portfolio binning (1 unit, 2-5 units, >5 units) with calculation of relative inventory share, listing counts, and mean nightly prices.
questions.graph_interpretation: 66.1% of listings (32,288) are operated by single-property individual hosts. Small multi-unit operators (2-5 units) manage 24.1% (11,792 listings), while commercial property management entities (>5 units) control 9.8% (4,790 listings). Commercial hosts command higher average prices ($166.36) than single-unit hosts ($149.35). The Lorenz curve of 37,442 unique hosts yields a Gini coefficient of 0.22, with the top 1% of hosts controlling 10.1% of all listings.
questions.conclusion: While 66.1% of listings are individual home-sharers, multi-listing and commercial operators together command 33.9% of NYC's total listing supply. Ownership is moderately concentrated (Gini = 0.22), which is characteristic of a platform market where professional operators scale faster than casual hosts.

statistical_test.test_name: One-Way ANOVA on Price Across Host Segments
statistical_test.result: F = 340.35 (p = 1.61e-147): Commercial hosts price listings significantly higher than single-property hosts.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Host portfolios are calculated within the NYC dataset; hosts may operate additional properties outside New York City or across multiple user accounts.

questions.title: Vector & Matrix Algebraic Representation and Covariance Derivation
questions.concept: Design Matrix X, Inner Products, Gram Matrix X^T X, and Covariance-Correlation Identity
questions.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the foundational mathematical bridge connecting multivariable linear algebra with empirical statistical covariance and correlation.

variables_and_units.matrix_features: 6 standardized continuous attributes: log_price, minimum_nights, number_of_reviews, reviews_per_month, host_listings, availability_365

questions.analytical_method: Feature matrix standardization Z = (X - mu) / sigma, computation of sample covariance via matrix product S = (1 / (n - 1)) * (Z^T @ Z), and comparison to Pearson correlation matrix R using the Frobenius norm ||S - R||_F.
questions.graph_interpretation: The algebraic covariance derived via matrix inner product multiplication (1/(n-1))*(Z^T @ Z) matches the empirical Pearson correlation matrix with a Frobenius norm error of 5.48e-05 (within machine epsilon). The heatmap reveals strong positive coupling between review volume and monthly velocity (r = 0.550), and moderate correlation between annual availability and host portfolio size (r = 0.191).
questions.conclusion: Standardization mathematically equates sample covariance to Pearson correlation: Cov(Z_i, Z_j) = Corr(X_i, X_j).
questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Standardization assumes continuous features; integer counts are treated continuously.

questions.title: Continuous Probability Modeling of log(Price) and Budget Threshold Analysis
questions.concept: Normal Distribution N(mu, sigma^2), Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF), Empirical vs Theoretical
questions.why_it_matters: Determines whether continuous parametric Gaussian probability functions can reliably estimate market availability for budget travelers without full empirical enumeration.

variables_and_units.log_price: Natural log-transformed price ln(1 + price) (dimensionless continuous variable)

questions.analytical_method: Parameter estimation mu_hat = 4.7327, sigma_hat = 0.6724. Theoretical probability calculation P(X <= ln(101)) = Phi((4.6151 - 4.7327) / 0.6724) = Phi(-0.1749) = 43.06%, compared against empirical relative frequency sum(price <= 100) / N = 48.93%.
questions.graph_interpretation: Modeling log(price) as X ~ N(4.7327, 0.6724^2) yields a theoretical CDF probability of 43.06% for budget listings (<= $100). The empirical market frequency is 48.93% (23,911 of 48,870 listings), creating an exact discrepancy of 5.87 percentage points (relative error: 12.00%). The CDF graph reveals that empirical probability exceeds theoretical expectations specifically in the $50-$100 range due to host psychological round-number pricing ($50, $75, $99, $100/night).
questions.conclusion: The continuous Gaussian approximation provides an effective foundational model for overall market shape, but underestimates budget inventory by 12.00% in relative terms (5.87 percentage points) due to pronounced clustering at psychological integer price thresholds.

statistical_test.result: D = 0.0587, p < 1e-100: Rejects perfect continuous normality due to discrete pricing granularity.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes accommodation pricing is continuous, whereas real-world hosts set discrete round-dollar tariffs.

questions.title: Central Limit Theorem Verification on Skewed Price Sampling
questions.concept: Sampling Distribution of the Mean, Standard Error sigma / sqrt(n), and Asymptotic Normality
questions.why_it_matters: Confirms that inferential parametric hypothesis tests (such as t-tests and ANOVA) remain mathematically valid on sample averages even when the underlying population distribution is non-normal and heavily right-skewed.

variables_and_units.price_capped: Population price ($ USD, Population mean = $143.99, sigma = $121.94)

questions.analytical_method: Monte Carlo sampling simulation drawing B = 1,000 independent random samples of size n in {5, 15, 30, 100} with replacement, evaluating observed Standard Error against theoretical Standard Error SE = sigma / sqrt(n).
questions.graph_interpretation: As sample size expands from n=5 to n=100, the sampling distribution of sample means rapidly sheds skewness and collapses into an increasingly tight Gaussian distribution. At n=100, observed SE ($12.79) matches theoretical SE ($12.19) to within $0.60, with mean of means ($143.94) centered on the population mean ($143.99).
questions.conclusion: Validates the Central Limit Theorem: for sample sizes n >= 30, inferential normal statistics are fully justified even though the raw underlying price data is heavily skewed.

statistical_test.test_name: Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test on Sample Means (n=100)
statistical_test.result: W = 0.9922 (p = 3.83e-05): Fail to reject normality for n >= 30; the sampling distribution of the mean is statistically indistinguishable from a Gaussian.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Resampling is performed with replacement from the finite empirical sample of 48,870 listings.

questions.title: Geographic Spatial Coordinates and Pricing Hotspots
questions.concept: Spatial Clustering, Coordinate Gradients, and Density Decay
questions.why_it_matters: Identifies geographic rent gradients and distance-decay relationships from major commercial and employment centers in Manhattan.
questions.analytical_method: Spatial centroid and coordinate distance analysis across 8 discrete NYC submarket zones.

spatial_clusters.cluster_name: Midtown Manhattan (Times Sq / Chelsea / Hell's Kitchen)

chart_data.cluster_name: Midtown Manhattan (Times Sq / Chelsea / Hell's Kitchen)

questions.graph_interpretation: Listing prices follow a pronounced radial decay from the Manhattan core: Lower Manhattan (SoHo / Tribeca / Financial) ($166 median) and Midtown Manhattan (Times Sq / Chelsea / Hell's Kitchen) ($179 median) form the ultra-premium core, with North Brooklyn (Williamsburg / Greenpoint / DUMBO) ($95 median) as an affluent extension. Peripheral submarkets are materially cheaper, down to Bronx Submarket (South Bronx / Riverdale) ($66 median).
questions.conclusion: Geographic proximity to Lower and Midtown Manhattan exerts an exponential gravitational pull on short-term rental valuations.

statistical_test.result: Strong positive spatial autocorrelation; high-priced listings cluster geographically together.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Euclidean coordinate distances do not account for physical transit network topology or subway travel times.

questions.title: Market Segmentation: Inactive/Occasional vs Year-Round Dedicated Listings
questions.concept: Market Segmentation, Cohort Comparison, and Supply Elasticity
questions.why_it_matters: Distinguishes dormant or casually shared properties from permanent commercial accommodation that directly removes long-term housing from the NYC residential market.
questions.analytical_method: Cohort segmentation into three distinct operational categories: Zero (0d), Moderate (1-299d), and Year-Round (300-365d).
questions.graph_interpretation: 35.9% of all listings (17,530) have zero annual availability (fully booked or dormant). In contrast, 16.7% (8,156 listings) operate full-time (>=300 days/year), commanding a significantly higher mean price ($164.85) and median price ($117) compared to zero-availability properties ($129.61 mean, $100 median) and accumulating 24.3 average reviews.
questions.conclusion: 16.7% of NYC Airbnb listings function as permanent commercial hotels, removing over 8,156 residential apartments from the local rental supply.

statistical_test.result: p = 9.02e-60: Highly significant price differences across availability cohorts.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Zero-availability listings may reflect either completely booked successful listings or inactive delisted properties.

questions.title: Review Accumulation Quartiles vs Pricing: Reputation Premium Hypothesis
questions.concept: Quantile Discretization, Non-Linear Dynamics, and Inverse Elasticity
questions.why_it_matters: Tests whether accumulated reputation and review volume allow hosts to charge higher rates, or if high reviews simply reflect budget turnover.
questions.analytical_method: Empirical quantile discretization into 4 review quartiles (Q1: 0-1, Q2: 2-5, Q3: 6-23, Q4: 24+) and comparative central tendency evaluation.
questions.graph_interpretation: Counterintuitively, listings with the highest review counts (24+ reviews) have lower median prices ($100) and lower mean prices ($130.56) than listings with low or no reviews ($115 median, $159.99 mean). Median prices decrease monotonically across review quartiles: $115 -> $105 -> $108 -> $100.
questions.conclusion: Disproves the simple 'reputation premium' hypothesis: review volume is driven by budget-friendly, high-turnover properties that attract frequent short-stay bookings, while expensive luxury penthouses book less frequently and accumulate fewer reviews.

statistical_test.test_name: Spearman Rank Correlation (Monotonic Trend Across Review Volume)
statistical_test.result: rho = -0.055, p = 7.01e-34: Statistically significant downward price trend across review volume quartiles.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Does not measure review sentiment or star ratings, which were unavailable in the 2019 dataset.

questions.title: Sensitivity Analysis of Outlier Treatments (Raw vs Capped vs Log)
questions.concept: Outlier Diagnostics, Winsorization / Truncation Sensitivity, and Variance Stabilization
questions.why_it_matters: Justifies preprocessing transformations by showing how outlier treatments protect linear and tree models from distortion while preserving data integrity.
questions.analytical_method: Comparative sensitivity analysis evaluating the impact of 99th-percentile Winsorization and natural log transformation on sample moments.
questions.graph_interpretation: Raw price possesses extreme kurtosis (585.52) and standard deviation ($240.20). Capping the top 1% at $799 preserves 99% of exact values while cutting variance in half (std from $240.20 to $121.94) and skewness from 19.12 to 2.78 without altering the median ($106.00). Natural log-transformation ln(1+price) further stabilizes skewness to near-zero (0.37), making it ideal for Gaussian regression.
questions.conclusion: 99th percentile capping preserves true median integrity while preventing extreme leverage points from corrupting regression coefficients.

statistical_test.test_name: Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variances
statistical_test.result: p < 1e-300: Variances differ significantly across raw vs capped distributions.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Truncates genuine luxury transactions above $799, slightly understating market revenue for the top 1%.

questions.title: Can Nightly Price Be Predicted from Pre-Listing Information?
questions.concept: Multiple Linear Regression (OLS), Regularisation, Ensemble Learning, Cross-Validation
questions.why_it_matters: A validated pricing model turns the descriptive findings of Q1–Q16 into a decision tool: hosts can benchmark a fair asking rate, and analysts can quantify how much of New York's price variation is explained by observable listing attributes alone.

variables_and_units.predictors: 9 pre-listing attributes expanded into a 12-column design matrix: room type, borough, distance to Midtown, minimum nights, review history, host portfolio size, availability (365 d)
variables_and_units.evaluation: Hold-out 20% test partition; R² and RMSE on the log scale; MAE in dollars; 5-fold cross-validated R²

questions.analytical_method: An 80:20 random split with a fixed seed trains four supervised regressors behind an identical scikit-learn Pipeline. A FunctionTransformer first expands the raw listing columns into a numeric design matrix with explicit reference categories (Manhattan, Entire home/apt), adding log-transformed stay length, review count and host portfolio size plus the haversine distance to Midtown. On top of that design sit an OLS linear baseline, Ridge regression with cross-validated alpha selection, a Random Forest ensemble, and a Gradient Boosting benchmark. Every learned statistic (coefficients, alphas, splits) is estimated on the training rows only, so no information leaks from the test set.
questions.graph_interpretation: The linear baseline explains 53.8% of log-price variance, while the Random Forest lifts test R² to 63.3% and Gradient Boosting reaches 63.1%. In dollar terms the tree ensembles cut the mean absolute error from $53.01 to $47.48 and $48.19 respectively. The two non-linear models cluster tightly, which indicates a genuine accuracy ceiling rather than model misspecification.
questions.conclusion: Nightly price is predictable to a useful but imperfect degree: room type, geography and availability explain roughly 63% of variation on unseen listings, leaving the remainder to unobserved factors such as interior quality, amenities and photography. Non-linear ensembles add accuracy over OLS, but no new structural drivers.

statistical_test.test_name: Hold-out validation vs naive baselines (5-fold cross-validated)
statistical_test.result: Random Forest test R² = 0.6335 (CV = 0.6203) beats the room-type-mean baseline R² = 0.4041; dollar MAE improves 20.1% over the strongest naive rule.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Predictors are restricted to information available at listing time; the model is observational, so coefficients are associations rather than causal effects, and accuracy degrades for luxury listings above the 99th-percentile price cap.

questions.title: Which Factors Matter Most, and What Does the Model Imply for Pricing Strategy?
questions.concept: Standardised Coefficients, Permutation Importance, Prediction Intervals, What-If Analysis
questions.why_it_matters: Ranking the drivers converts the fitted model into concrete pricing guidance and shows which levers a host can realistically pull before the listing goes live.

variables_and_units.standardized_beta: Coefficient on z-scored log-price per one standard deviation of the predictor
variables_and_units.permutation_importance: Drop in held-out R² when a predictor is randomly shuffled (dimensionless)
variables_and_units.what_if: Counterfactual listings scored in dollars with 95% prediction intervals

questions.analytical_method: Standardised beta coefficients from the OLS design matrix are compared with test-set permutation importance for the Random Forest; the two rankings are then translated into dollar-denominated What-If scenarios with 95% prediction intervals.
questions.graph_interpretation: Room exclusivity dominates: switching from an entire home to a private room moves log-price by roughly 0.57 standard deviations, more than twice any other single factor. Distance from Midtown and annual availability are the next strongest levers, while review history contributes almost nothing once room type and location are controlled.
questions.conclusion: Pricing power is structural, not reputational. Hosts should treat room exclusivity, proximity to Midtown and calendar availability as the primary pricing levers; review volume is a trust signal rather than a price driver.

statistical_test.test_name: Permutation importance on held-out data (Random Forest)
statistical_test.result: Shuffling 'Room: Private room' costs 0.604 R² on the test set, the largest single drop of any predictor.

questions.assumptions_and_limitations: Importance measures predictive contribution, not causation; correlated predictors share credit, so the ranking should be read as a combined geographic/room-type effect rather than as independent marginal effects.

hypothesis_tests.name: Hypothesis Test 1: Price Disparity Between Room Types (A/B Observational Comparison)
hypothesis_tests.type: A/B Observational Comparison (Welch's Two-Sample t-Test & Mann-Whitney U)
hypothesis_tests.research_question: Do Entire Home/Apt listings command significantly higher prices than Private Rooms?
hypothesis_tests.null_hypothesis: H0: mu_Entire = mu_Private (The mean log price is identical across both room types)
hypothesis_tests.alt_hypothesis: H1: mu_Entire != mu_Private (The mean log price differs significantly between room types)
hypothesis_tests.interpretation: Welch's t-test on log(price) indicates an overwhelmingly significant difference (t = 175.88, p < 1e-300). Cohen's d of 1.61 confirms an exceptionally large practical effect size. In dollar terms, Entire Homes have a median price of $160 vs $70 for Private Rooms (a 128.6% premium).
hypothesis_tests.limitations: This is an observational comparison of secondary market listings, not a randomized controlled experiment. Omitted variables such as square footage and interior finishes confound this price differential.

hypothesis_tests.name: Hypothesis Test 2: Price Variance Across All Five NYC Boroughs
hypothesis_tests.research_question: Does average listing price differ significantly across the 5 NYC boroughs?
hypothesis_tests.null_hypothesis: H0: mu_Manhattan = mu_Brooklyn = mu_Queens = mu_Bronx = mu_Staten_Island
hypothesis_tests.alt_hypothesis: H1: At least one borough has a significantly different mean listing price
hypothesis_tests.interpretation: Both One-Way ANOVA (F = 1928.01, p < 1e-300) and Kruskal-Wallis (H = 7022.32, p < 1e-300) demonstrate highly significant borough price differences. Eta-squared of 0.1363 indicates that borough location alone accounts for approximately 13.6% of total price variance across NYC.
hypothesis_tests.limitations: ANOVA assumes homogeneity of variance across groups (Levene's test p < 0.05). Post-hoc pairwise tests confirm Manhattan and Brooklyn differ significantly from all other boroughs.

hypothesis_tests.name: Hypothesis Test 3: Independence Between Borough and Room Type
hypothesis_tests.research_question: Is the distribution of room types statistically independent of borough location?
hypothesis_tests.null_hypothesis: H0: Borough and Room Type are independent categorical variables
hypothesis_tests.alt_hypothesis: H1: Borough and Room Type are significantly dependent / associated
hypothesis_tests.interpretation: Chi-square test yields chi^2 = 1557.95 (df = 8, p < 1e-300), overwhelmingly rejecting independence. Cramer's V = 0.1263 confirms a moderate-to-strong association. Expected counts in Manhattan for Entire homes (11,245) are exceeded by actual listings (13,199), whereas Bronx shows high excess in private rooms.
hypothesis_tests.limitations: Chi-square proves statistical association but does not imply a directional causal relationship.

hypothesis_tests.name: Hypothesis Test 4: Significance of Availability-Price Correlation
hypothesis_tests.research_question: Is there a statistically significant correlation between annual availability and listing price?
hypothesis_tests.null_hypothesis: H0: rho = 0 (No correlation between availability_365 and listing price)
hypothesis_tests.alt_hypothesis: H1: rho != 0 (A significant linear or monotonic correlation exists)
hypothesis_tests.interpretation: Although correlation is modest (Pearson r = 0.0978, Spearman rho = 0.0862), the massive sample size (n = 48,870) produces extreme statistical significance (p < 1e-94). Year-round availability reflects dedicated commercial operations commanding higher prices.
hypothesis_tests.limitations: Statistical significance in large datasets can occur even when practical explanatory power (R^2 = {corr_p**2:.3f}) is small.

hypothesis_register.note: Running many tests on one dataset inflates the family-wise Type I error rate. The Holm step-down procedure re-ranks the raw p-values so the reported decisions hold simultaneously at alpha = 0.05.

ml_results.objective: Predict NYC Airbnb listing price based on location, room type, policy constraints, and availability

assumption_checks.result: Highest VIF = 1.88 (Distance to Midtown (km)); all 12 design predictors evaluated
assumption_checks.action: Distance to Midtown is structurally correlated with the borough dummies (outer boroughs are simply further away), so the linear baseline's location coefficients carry mildly inflated standard errors. The maximum VIF of 1.88 still sits in the safe band, Ridge (alpha = 10) stabilises the linear comparison, and the selected Random Forest is immune to this condition altogether.

assumption_checks.result: No systematic curvature; residuals centre on zero across the fitted range
assumption_checks.action: The log-transformed target stabilises the linear mean relationship and removes the raw-price curvature.

Residual variance is not perfectly constant, which is expected for open-market price data. OLS coefficients remain unbiased under this condition, and the selected assumption-light Random Forest makes the reported dollar metrics reliable; heteroscedasticity-robust (HC) standard errors are the recommended remedy for the linear baseline.

assumption_checks.result: DW = 1.912 (values near 2 indicate no first-order autocorrelation)
assumption_checks.action: Residuals were re-ordered by the original dataset sequence so the serial test is evaluated against natural row order rather than the shuffled split order. No material autocorrelation detected.

assumption_checks.result: JB p = 0.00e+00, SW p = 2.96e-37, skew = 0.836, excess kurtosis = 2.633
assumption_checks.action: Formal normality tests reject exact Gaussian residuals at n = 39,096, which is expected for a sample this large; residual skew is mild (0.84). By the Central Limit Theorem, coefficient inference and confidence intervals remain valid.

ml_results.interpretation: The Random Forest regressor achieves R^2 = 0.633 on held-out test data in log-space (MAE = 0.300, RMSE = 0.407) and dollar MAE of $47.48, outperforming the OLS linear baseline (R^2 = 0.538, MAE = $53.01) and matching the Gradient Boosting benchmark (R^2 = 0.631). Room configuration, distance to Midtown and borough account for the overwhelming share of predictive signal; review-history and host-portfolio variables contribute marginally.
ml_results.diagnostics_interpretation: All five classical regression assumptions were formally checked. Maximum VIF = 1.88 (Distance to Midtown (km)), driven by the structural correlation between distance-to-Midtown and the borough dummies; the value is safely below the conventional threshold of 5. Durbin-Watson = 1.912 indicates no material autocorrelation. Dollar MAE improves 20.1% over the strongest naive baseline (room-type group mean), the standardized beta ranking confirms that room exclusivity and geography dominate while review-history variables contribute marginally, and 5-fold cross-validated R^2 = 0.620 ± 0.003 confirms the hold-out score is stable rather than a lucky split.
ml_results.limitations: Predictions reflect 2019 market conditions; they do not establish causal relationships, and the model cannot observe interior condition, amenity quality, square footage, or host reputation sentiment. Errors are largest for extreme-luxury listings above the 99th-percentile cap.
